To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
excessive fructose consumption, especially in the form of sugar-sweetened beverages, may be the primary dietary cause of type 2 diabetes.
the ingestion of excessive amounts of fructose, which is a component of sugar and high fructose syrup, may cause type 2 diabetic mellitus.

fructose induces features associated with metabolic syndrome, including hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia, hyperleptinemia, insulin resistance, and hyperuricemia, and these features are mediated in part by uric acid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the hypothesis that excessive fructose consumption is a major cause of metabolic syndrome and diabetes.
the potential role of excessive fructose intake as one of the underlying causes of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.
the hypothesis that excessive fructose ingestion and uric acid might be one of the primary underlying causes of metabolic syndrome and diabetes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
excessive fructose consumption, in the presence of a genetic susceptibility, may be an underlying cause of the epidemic of obesity and type 2 DM.
fructose intake and/or uric acid are associated with metabolic syndrome and type II diabetes.
the ingestion of excessive amounts of fructose is a risk factor for the development of diabetes and metabolic syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
excessive fructose consumption is a major cause of metabolic syndrome and diabetes.
fructose intake and hyperuricemia are two important factors in the development of metabolic syndrome and diabetes.
fructose and uric acid are two of the underlying etiological factors of the metabolic syndrome, and both are preventable and treatable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
fructose is a unique sugar that is not equivalent to other sugars.
the ingestion of excessive amounts of fructose may contribute to metabolic syndrome and type II diabetes.
the public health community should consider reducing fructose consumption to <50 g/d, and this would be especially true for those with diabetes or metabolic syndrome.
